title: Stare at a waterfall for a minute, and the rocks beside it seem to drift upwards

cover.alt: The Falls of Foyers in the Scottish Highlands: a tall white waterfall pouring down a dark rock gorge into a pool, framed by green trees.

body: This is the motion aftereffect. In 1834 Robert Addams described it after watching the Falls of Foyers near Loch Ness: when he looked away from the falling water at the rocks beside it, they seemed to creep upwards. The likely reason is adaptation. Neurons that signal one direction of movement respond less and less while that movement goes on. A still scene is normally seen as still because the signals for every direction balance out, so after a minute of downward motion the balance tips the other way and stationary rock appears to rise.

slides.heading: Why still rocks seem to rise

steps.label: Watch water falling for about a minute
Neurons for downward motion respond less
Look at the still rocks beside it
The rocks appear to drift upwards

left.label: What you see
left.text: Rocks, moss and trees slowly sliding upwards, though nothing in the scene is moving.

right.label: What’s happening
right.text: Your motion detectors have adapted to the fall of water, so a motionless view reads as movement the other way.

slides.heading: Who noticed what
slides.explanation: Aristotle reported the effect without saying which way things moved. Purkyně gave the first clear description; ‘waterfall illusion’ was coined in 1880.

slides.prompt: Stare at the centre of a rotating spiral for a while, then look at a still pattern. What does the pattern seem to do?
slides.detail: This is the spiral aftereffect, the same adaptation at work: whatever motion you watched, stillness afterwards looks like motion in the reverse direction.

slides.heading: Any steady motion will do
slides.text: The effect is not special to water. Purkyně noticed it after watching a cavalry parade go by, and a rotating spiral produces a version of it too. Viewing motion for anything from tens of milliseconds to minutes can leave an aftereffect.
